title: Food of the English-Speaking World
description: Ten standalone texts about the food of the English-speaking world and its history, from Southern biscuits and the Cornish pasty to damper, soda bread, maple syrup, the hāngī, shortbread and a Caribbean Sunday lunch in London.

lessons.title: Biscuits Before Baking Powder
lessons.summary: In eastern Tennessee, a grandmother teaches her grandson to make Southern biscuits and sausage gravy and tells him how biscuits were made before baking powder.
lessons.text:
My grandmother has made biscuits every weekday morning for sixty years. Her kitchen in the hills of eastern Tennessee is small and bright, and by six o'clock it smells of butter, black pepper and coffee. When I stayed with her last spring, I asked her to teach me. She does not teach just anyone; she must first deem you serious, and it took her two days to deem me serious enough.

A Southern biscuit is not the hard, sweet biscuit that people in Britain eat with tea. It is a soft, tender bread, closer to a scone, meant to be broken open while it is still hot. My grandmother makes hers with flour, cold butter and buttermilk, and she raises them with baking powder from a red can. She never twists the cutter, because a twist seals the edges and keeps the biscuits from rising.

Baking powder, she told me, is younger than it looks. It became common in kitchens across the United States only in the second half of the nineteenth century. Before that, many Southern cooks made beaten biscuits. They whacked the stiff dough with a rolling pin for half an hour or more, folding it over and whacking it again until air was trapped inside. Other cooks used pearlash, a white powder made from wood ashes, which chemists call potassium carbonate. In 1796, Amelia Simmons called for pearlash in the first cookbook written by a native of the young United States, and historians see this potassium salt as a precursor of baking soda and baking powder.

My grandmother owns a reprint of that little book. The reprint was cheap and its cover is torn, but she keeps it beside her Bible.

The gravy is simpler still. She browns sausage in a heavy iron pan, lifts the meat out, and stirs flour into the fat. Then she pours in milk slowly, stirring all the time, until the gravy is thick, pale and full of pepper. Many people in the South call it sawmill gravy, after a popular story that it fed the men of the logging camps in the mountains. Nobody can prove the story, but it is a good one.

On a weekday, biscuits and gravy are a quick breakfast before work. On Sundays, the meal grows. On the Sunday before I left, she made fried chicken, lima beans, which she calls butter beans, and a basket of hush puppies, small balls of fried cornmeal. Her old dog sat by my chair and whined, and she hushed him with a single word.

When I packed the car, she gave me her recipe on a card. It was conveniently short: flour, butter, buttermilk, a hot oven and, at the bottom, "Don't twist." She had also, conveniently, packed six biscuits for the drive.

Questions:
Why does the grandmother never twist the cutter?
A twist seals the edges and keeps the biscuits from rising.
How did cooks make beaten biscuits before baking powder?
They whacked the stiff dough with a rolling pin for half an hour or more, until air was trapped inside.
What is pearlash, and why do historians find it interesting?
Pearlash is potassium carbonate, a powder made from wood ashes, and historians see it as a precursor of baking soda and baking powder.
Where does the grandmother keep her reprint of the old cookbook?
She keeps the reprint beside her Bible.
What does she call lima beans?
She calls them butter beans.

lessons.title: The Pasty and the Miners
lessons.summary: A visitor to Cornwall learns how the pasty became the meal of the tin miners and how it won protected status.
lessons.text:
Every summer, the seaside towns of Cornwall, at the far southwestern tip of England, receive an influx of visitors. They arrive by train, by bus and in convertibles with the roof down, and many of them have one meal in mind before they even see the sea: a Cornish pasty, eaten warm from a paper bag on a harbor wall.

A pasty is a round of pastry folded over a filling and sealed with a thick, twisted edge called the crimp. The filling of a true Cornish pasty is raw beef, potato, onion and swede, the yellow root that cooks in the United States call rutabaga, seasoned with salt and pepper. Carrots are considered improper, and many Cornish bakers will tell you that an improper pasty is not a pasty at all.

Pies of this kind were eaten all over medieval England, by kings as well as farm workers, but by the nineteenth century the pasty belonged above all to the tin and copper miners of Cornwall. A miner could carry a pasty underground and eat it hours later, still warm, in the dark. A popular story says that the thick crimp served as a handle, so that a man with dirty hands could hold the pasty by its edge and throw that part away. Another says that fearful miners left a piece of crust for the knockers, the spirits who were believed to live in the mines and who had to be kept in a good mood. Historians are cautious about both stories, but men who worked far below the ground had every reason to be fearful.

When many Cornish mines closed in the nineteenth century, thousands of miners left for mines in North America, South Africa and Australia, and they took the pasty with them. It is still sold in the old mining towns of Michigan.

For the pasty at home, 2011 was a watershed. In that year, the European Union gave the Cornish pasty protected status, which means that only pasties made in Cornwall, to the traditional recipe, may be sold under that name. For small artisan bakers, it was a watershed in another sense as well: it turned a local habit into protected heritage.

In a small harbor town, where fishing boats lie in their berths and the beach is made of smooth gray pebbles, I bought a pasty from one such artisan. She starts work at four in the morning, because the summer influx keeps her busy until dark. Her window also held a tray of rum babas, which she makes for the visitors, and she admitted that the babas sell almost as well as the pasties. I carried my pasty down to the beach, sat on the warm pebbles, and watched a boat ease into its berth while I ate.

Questions:
Why are the seaside towns of Cornwall busy every summer?
They receive an influx of visitors, who arrive by train, by bus and in convertibles.
What goes into a true Cornish pasty?
Raw beef, potato, onion and swede go into it, with salt and pepper.
Why might the miners have left a piece of crust for the knockers?
The miners were fearful, and the knockers were spirits who had to be kept in a good mood.
Why was 2011 a watershed for the pasty?
In that year it received protected status, so only pasties made in Cornwall to the traditional recipe may carry the name.

lessons.title: Damper by the Waterhole
lessons.summary: On a camping trip in the outback, Tom shows his daughter Megan how to bake damper in the coals of a campfire.
lessons.text:
Late in the afternoon, Megan and her father, Tom, reached the waterhole and stopped the car beneath a canopy of river red gums. They had driven for six hours through the flat red country of western New South Wales, where low gray shrubs of saltbush stretched to the horizon. After so much dry land, the waterhole felt like an oasis.

Tom had promised to make damper, the bread of the Australian bush. While Megan collected sticks, he explained its history. In the nineteenth century, stockmen who drove cattle over great distances, and swagmen who walked from farm to farm looking for work, carried flour, salt and tea, because those things kept for weeks and weighed little. With water and a fire, the flour became damper: a plain, heavy loaf baked in the hot ashes. Long before that, Aboriginal peoples had ground seeds between stones to make their own breads, a practice that goes back many thousands of years.

Tom built the fire and let it burn down. Damper needs coals, not flames, he said, and a good bed of coals looks almost like charcoal, black on the outside and glowing red beneath. He mixed flour, salt and water in a metal bowl until he had a soft dough, shaped it into a round, and laid it in the coals. Then he raked more coals and ashes over the top. He said that the bits of charcoal stuck to the crust were part of the flavor.

While the damper baked, he filled the billy, the tin can with a wire handle that serves as a kettle in the bush, and hung it at the edge of the fire. The kettle came to the boil slowly, and he threw in a handful of tea.

Megan sat on a log and watched a small flock of zebra finches come down to drink. The finches were tiny gray birds with bright orange beaks, and they drank silently at the edge of the water before flying back into the shrubs. Tom reminded her to watch where she put her feet, because brown snakes live in country like this, and their venom is among the most dangerous in the world. Snakes rarely bite unless they are disturbed, he said, so the best defense against venom is simply to leave them alone.

After half an hour, he knocked on the damper with a stick. It sounded hollow, which meant it was done. They ate it hot, with butter and golden syrup, as the sky turned pink and the birds settled silently into the canopy.

"At home we'd be having a barbie tonight," Tom said, using the word that many people in Australia use for a barbecue. "But damper beats a barbie." Megan, whose mouth was full, agreed.

Questions:
Why did the waterhole feel like an oasis?
After six hours of dry land, the water and the shade felt like an oasis.
Why did stockmen and swagmen carry flour, salt and tea?
Those things kept for weeks and weighed little.
How did Tom bake the damper?
He laid the dough in a bed of hot coals and covered it with more coals and ashes.
What did Tom say about snake venom?
Snakes rarely bite unless they are disturbed, so the best defense against venom is to leave them alone.
How did Tom know that the damper was done?
He knocked on it with a stick, and it sounded hollow.

lessons.title: Soda Bread on a Wet Afternoon
lessons.summary: A retired teacher in Ireland shows the narrator how to make soda bread and farls, and explains where the bread comes from.
lessons.text:
It rained all afternoon on the day Bridget Quinn taught me to make soda bread, and it was the right weather for it. Soda bread is the bread of wet days and busy kitchens, of days when there is no time to wait for yeast. Bridget is eighty-one, a retired schoolteacher with a cameo pinned to her sweater, and she has made the same loaf so often that she no longer needs a recipe. She learned it as a girl, and she expected me to memorize it too.

"Flour, soda, salt, buttermilk," she said. "Four things. If you can't memorize four things, you shouldn't be in a kitchen."

Baking soda reached Irish kitchens only in the middle of the nineteenth century. Irish wheat is soft and makes poor yeast bread, but the soda, mixed with sour buttermilk, makes gas, and the gas lifts the dough as it bakes. For families who cooked over an open fire, in an iron pot with a lid, it was a quick and reliable way to have fresh bread every day.

Bridget mixed the dough with one hand and touched it as little as possible. Then she shaped a round and cut a deep cross into the top. I asked whether the cross was a blessing or, as the old story says, a way to let the fairies out. "It's a way to let the heat in," she said, "but I won't stop anyone blessing it." She has a jolly laugh, and she used it often that afternoon.

She also showed me the griddle bread of the north. She patted a round of dough flat and cut it into four quarters, which are called farls; the word comes from an old Scots word meaning a fourth part. The quartet of farls cooked on a dry pan until they were brown on both sides. In Belfast, she said, a quartet of farls fried in butter is part of a proper breakfast.

Above her table, a faded card was tacked to a cork board. It was her mother's recipe for spotted dog, the festive soda bread with raisins and sugar that many families bake at Christmas. She did not need to read it, she said, but she liked to see her mother's handwriting. Then she told me, with another jolly laugh, about the year she let a nephew bake the Christmas loaf and he forgot the soda. "I still rue that day," she said. "You could have built a wall with that bread."

As the loaf cooled, she grew quiet and reflective. She said that the cameo had been a gift from her husband, who loved soda bread more than cake. The loaf I carried home had cost a few cents to make, but the afternoon was priceless. A reflective hour in a warm kitchen on a wet day is a priceless gift to give a stranger.

Questions:
What four things go into Bridget's soda bread?
Flour, soda, salt and buttermilk go into it.
Why did soda bread suit Irish kitchens so well?
Irish wheat is soft and makes poor yeast bread, but soda and buttermilk lift the dough quickly.
What is tacked to the cork board above Bridget's table?
Her mother's recipe for spotted dog, the festive soda bread made at Christmas, is tacked there.
Why does Bridget still rue one Christmas?
Her nephew baked the Christmas loaf and forgot the soda.

lessons.title: Sugaring Season
lessons.summary: Julie helps her uncle Marc in his sugar bush in Quebec, where sap flows through tubing to the sugar shack and becomes maple syrup.
lessons.text:
In late March, when the nights are still freezing but daytime temperatures rise above zero, Julie drives from Montreal to her uncle Marc's sugar bush in the Beauce, south of Quebec City. A sugar bush is a forest of sugar maples, and in spring it is the busiest place in Marc's life.

Long before Europeans arrived, the Indigenous peoples of the region, among them the Anishinaabe and the Haudenosaunee, cut into the bark of maple trees, collected the sweet sap, and boiled it down into sugar. French settlers learned the practice from them. For centuries, sap was collected in buckets hung on the trees. Today, on a farm like Marc's, a network of blue plastic tubing runs from tree to tree and down the hill to the sugar shack. The lines follow a gentle gradient, so that the sap flows downhill on its own, and a vacuum pump helps it along. Marc spent years getting the gradient right. If the slope is too flat, the sap sits in the tubes; if it is too steep, the lines pull loose.

Julie's first job every morning is to walk the lines and look for problems. A fallen branch can put a kink in a tube, and a single kink can stop the flow from fifty trees. When Marc rides out on his four-wheeler, he keeps his thumb on the throttle and eases the throttle back on the icy slopes, because the snow hides the tubes.

Sap contains only two or three percent sugar, so it takes about forty liters of sap to make one liter of syrup. In the sugar shack, the sap is boiled in a long, flat pan until the water has gone and the syrup is thick and golden. One morning the pump suffered a malfunction, and for an anxious hour the sap stopped moving. Marc found the cause, a frozen valve, and fixed the malfunction with a hair dryer.

Quebec produces about seventy percent of the world's maple syrup, and its producers have organized their industry in an unusual way. Instead of letting thousands of farms vie with one another on price, their federation runs a centralized system: it sets limits on how much each farm may sell and keeps a large reserve of syrup in barrels, which it releases in poor years. Some farmers dislike the centralized model; others say it keeps prices steady. Marc would rather vie with other farms over quality.

On weekends, the sugar shack opens to visitors, and Marc has to prioritize the guests over the trees. Julie has learned to prioritize the youngest children in the line. She dispenses hot syrup onto clean snow packed into a long wooden tray, and the children roll it onto sticks as it hardens into taffy. She dispenses one line of syrup after another, and the children's delight is contagious. By late afternoon even the most serious adults are laughing, because at a sugar shack, joy is contagious.

Questions:
Why does the tubing follow a gentle gradient?
The gradient lets the sap flow downhill on its own.
What can a single kink in a tube do?
A single kink can stop the flow from fifty trees.
How did Marc fix the malfunction of the pump?
He found a frozen valve and fixed it with a hair dryer.
Why do Quebec's maple farms not vie with one another on price?
Its federation runs a centralized system that limits sales and keeps a reserve of syrup.

lessons.title: Food from the Earth
lessons.summary: Aroha's family prepares a hāngī, a Māori earth oven, for her grandmother's eightieth birthday, and Aroha explains each step to a visitor.
lessons.text:
Before Aroha explains anything else to visitors, she teaches them to say the word properly. Hāngī has two syllables, and the small lines over its vowels show that both are long. The first syllable sounds like "hah," and the second begins with the soft "ng" of "singer." How you say a word, Aroha says, shows how much you respect the people it belongs to.

A hāngī is the traditional Māori way of cooking food in the earth. On the day I visited, Aroha's family was preparing one for her grandmother's eightieth birthday at their marae, the meeting place of the community. A hāngī feeds many people at once, so it belongs to large gatherings: birthdays, weddings, reunions, and also funerals, when the hosts feed the visitors who come to offer their condolences. Feeding those who come with condolences, Aroha explained, is part of how a community cares for its guests.

Work began before dawn. Her uncles dug a pit, which is harder than it looks; by the time it was deep enough, her cousin said that his abdominal muscles ached more than his arms. Digging and lifting, he discovered, are abdominal work. Then the uncles built a large fire and heated stones in it for several hours. Volcanic stones are preferred because they hold heat well. River stones can hold water inside them, and when they are heated, the water turns to steam and the stone may break apart, with catastrophic results for anyone standing close. Aroha's uncles have used the same stones for years and treat them with care.

Meanwhile, the food was made ready: pork, chicken, lamb, pumpkin, potato and kūmara, the sweet potato. In the past, food was wrapped in leaves and placed in baskets woven from flax, a plant that grows in the wetlands of New Zealand. Today most families use wire baskets and foil, and they cover the food with cloths immersed in water. Aroha immersed the cloths in a large tub until they were heavy and dripping.

When the stones were glowing, they were spread across the bottom of the pit, and the baskets were lowered onto them. The wet cloths went over the food, and earth was shoveled over everything to trap the steam. For three or four hours, the meal cooked under the ground.

The moment of uncovering is the best part. When the uncles lifted the last cloth, a cloud of steam rose from the pit, smelling of smoke and earth, and the children cheered. Aroha says that a hāngī does not so much cook food as unleash it: the slow, wet heat seems to unleash every flavor at once.

Aroha's grandmother has seen her language and customs grow weak and then return in her lifetime. She says that the hāngī teaches resilience: the right stones go into the fire again and again and do not break. The resilience of her people, she says, is like that.

Questions:
How many syllables does the word hāngī have?
It has two syllables, and both vowels are long.
Why can river stones be dangerous in a hāngī?
They can hold water, which turns to steam when heated and may break the stone, with catastrophic results.
Where does flax grow?
Flax grows in the wetlands of New Zealand.
What does the grandmother say the hāngī teaches?
She says it teaches resilience, because the right stones go into the fire again and again and do not break.

lessons.title: Granny Isla's Shortbread
lessons.summary: A young woman writes down her grandmother's shortbread recipe and learns where shortbread comes from.
lessons.text:
My grandmother, Isla, has made shortbread every December for seventy years. For many years her shortbread won first prize at the village show, usually by a landslide. The one year she lost, she lost to her own sister, and not by a landslide. Two years ago, she was told that she has Parkinson's disease, a neurological condition that makes her hands shake. She can no longer roll out dough, so this winter she asked me to bake, and to write the recipe down before it was lost.

The recipe existed only on a single card, written in pencil in her own brief style. My task was transcription: copying it out clearly so that the whole family could use it. The transcription turned out to be harder than I expected, because Isla does not believe in punctuation. One line read: "Rub in butter cold hands quick." Without a comma, I could not tell whether the butter had to be cold, or the hands, or both. I asked for clarification. "Both," she said. "Put a comma wherever you like."

The method is simple. One part sugar, two parts butter, three parts flour, with a little rice flour for crispness. The butter is rubbed into the flour by hand until the mixture looks like sand, and then it is pressed into a round tin, marked into wedges and baked slowly until it is pale gold. After twenty minutes of rubbing, my hand began to cramp, and Isla, watching from her chair, told me that a cramp was proof I was doing it properly. She spent the afternoon hectoring me from her chair, though always with a smile: colder butter, lighter fingers, lower oven. Her hectoring was the most useful part of the recipe.

While the shortbread baked, I asked her for one more clarification: why is it called short? The word, she said, means crumbly, as in "shortening." A dough that is rich in butter breaks easily, and that is what makes shortbread short. Its history goes back to the medieval biscuit bread of Scotland, which was leftover bread dough dried slowly in the oven. Over time, cooks replaced the yeast with butter, and the result became shortbread. A recipe was printed in Glasgow as early as 1736. There is also a story that Mary, Queen of Scots, loved a thin, fan-shaped kind called petticoat tails, but Isla treats that story the way she treats commas, as something optional.

Her neurological condition has changed many things, she told me, but not her memory for recipes, and not her opinions. When the shortbread came out, she tasted it slowly and declared it nearly as good as hers.

I typed the transcription that evening and sent it to every cousin, with a comma in every place where a comma could possibly go.

Questions:
Why can Isla no longer bake shortbread herself?
She has Parkinson's disease, a neurological condition that makes her hands shake.
Why was the transcription of the recipe difficult?
Isla does not use punctuation, so without a comma it was unclear what had to be cold.
What clarification did Isla give about the butter and the hands?
She said that both had to be cold.
What did Isla say about the cramp in her granddaughter's hand?
She said that a cramp was proof that she was doing it properly.
Why is shortbread called short?
Short means crumbly, and a dough rich in butter breaks easily.

lessons.title: Sunday Lunch in South London
lessons.summary: Kezia photographs her family's monthly Caribbean Sunday lunch at her grandparents' house in Brixton.
lessons.text:
On the first Sunday of every month, my grandparents' house in Brixton fills with family, and I bring my grandfather's old rangefinder camera to record it. The rangefinder is heavier than my phone and much slower, but Grandad says that a slow camera makes you look properly before you press the button, and he is usually right.

Grandad came to London from Jamaica in 1958, one of many thousands of people from the Caribbean who came to Britain after the war to work. He arrived in a gray, damp metropolis that was still repairing its bomb damage, and he says that the cold was his first shock and the food was his second. Gran came from Trinidad a year later. They met at a church dance, and sixty years on, the metropolis that once seemed so cold is the only home their grandchildren have known.

Lunch begins after church. Grandad still wears his church suit and the same cologne he has worn for forty years; when I was small, I thought that his cologne was simply what Sunday smelled like. Gran has been cooking since dawn. There is rice and peas, made with red kidney beans, coconut milk and fresh thyme, curry goat, fried plantain, a dish of baked macaroni pie from Trinidad, and brown stew chicken, which she rubs with lime juice before she cooks it. Citrus, she says, makes the meat taste clean, and she uses citrus in almost everything.

The table holds three generations and more than one story. My father is Gran and Grandad's son, and my mother grew up in Yorkshire. When they married, interracial couples were common enough in London that nobody at the wedding remarked on it, although Grandad remembers a time when an interracial couple would have been stared at in the street.

My youngest cousin, who is four, reached across the table and shouted, "Gimme plantain!" Gran put down her spoon. "Gimme is not a word at my table," she said, and he tried again with "please." My teenage cousin announced that macaroni pie was his fave. Gran said that fave was not much better than gimme, but that she would accept it from anyone who offered to wash the dishes.

After lunch, Grandad puts on his old records and tries to boogie in the living room, and the children try to boogie with him. Then come the leftovers. My aunt packs them into disposable boxes, and Gran, who washes and keeps every old ice cream tub, shakes her head at the disposable boxes every single month.

In August, the whole family goes to the Notting Hill Carnival, the great street pageant of costume, steel drums and food that grew out of Caribbean community events more than half a century ago. For Gran, the Sunday lunch is a smaller pageant of the same kind, and I photograph it with the same care.

Questions:
Why does Kezia use her grandfather's rangefinder camera?
Grandad says that a slow camera makes you look properly before you press the button.
What was London like when Grandad arrived?
It was a gray, damp metropolis that was still repairing its bomb damage.
Why does Gran use citrus in her cooking?
She says that citrus makes the meat taste clean.
What did Gran say when her youngest grandson said "gimme"?
She said that gimme is not a word at her table.
What is the Notting Hill Carnival?
It is a great street pageant of costume, steel drums and food every August.

lessons.title: The Earl and His Sandwich
lessons.summary: An essay on the Earl of Sandwich, the anecdote that gave his name to the sandwich, and what historians think of it.
lessons.text:
Few people have given their name to something eaten every day by millions. John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, who lived from 1718 to 1792, is one of them, and the story of how it happened is one of the most repeated anecdotes in the history of food.

The anecdote goes like this. The Earl, a passionate card player, once sat at the gaming table for twenty-four hours without a break. When he grew hungry, he refused to leave the game and asked for salt beef between two slices of toast, so that he could eat with one hand and play with the other. Soon others were asking for "the same as Sandwich." The story is attested by a French writer, Pierre-Jean Grosley, who visited London in 1765 and later described it in a book. The word itself is attested a little earlier: in 1762, the historian Edward Gibbon wrote in his diary that he had seen gentlemen at a London club eating cold meat, or "a Sandwich."

The anecdote fits the Earl's reputation as a playboy, a rich man who spent his nights at cards and his money on pleasure. Yet his modern biographer argues that the playboy picture is unfair. Sandwich was a serious, hard-working official. He left Eton and his alma mater, Trinity College, Cambridge, with a fine classical education and a love of music that lasted all his life. As a diplomat, he helped to negotiate the peace that ended a long European war in 1748. The treaty was signed that year, and the governments that had fought ratified it soon after; in an age of slow letters, ratifying a treaty could take weeks. He was three times First Lord of the Admiralty, the de facto head of the navy, and he supported the voyages of Captain James Cook, who named the Sandwich Islands, now Hawaii, after him. The biographer suggests that Sandwich more probably ate his beef and bread at his desk than at a card table.

The Earl had enemies, and they had grievances. In 1763 he attacked a former friend in Parliament over a rude poem, and many people called him a hypocrite, since his own private life was far from pure. Critics also blamed him for the weakness of the navy during the war with the colonies in North America. Their grievances were loud, and some were fair.

People had been eating bread with something inside it for thousands of years, and the Earl did not invent the habit. What his name did was to normalize it among the rich, and to normalize the idea that a meal could be eaten with the fingers, without leaving one's work or one's game.

Questions:
What does the famous anecdote say about the Earl?
It says that he ate salt beef between two slices of toast so that he could keep playing cards.
Who attests the story?
A French writer, Pierre-Jean Grosley, who visited London in 1765, attests it.
What did the Earl take from his alma mater?
He took a fine classical education and a lifelong love of music.
Why did many people call him a hypocrite?
He attacked a former friend over a rude poem, although his own private life was far from pure.
What made him the de facto head of the navy?
He was First Lord of the Admiralty.

lessons.title: Digging for Victory
lessons.summary: A community gardener remembers the wartime vegetable gardens of Britain and the United States while her own garden club plants lettuce.
lessons.text:
Every spring, our community garden sends a questionnaire to its members. It asks what they plan to grow, how much time they can give, and why they garden at all. This year, one older member answered the last question with two words: "My mother." Her mother, she explained, had grown vegetables in a London park during the war, and I have been reading about those wartime gardens ever since.

In Britain, the government began a campaign called Dig for Victory in 1939. Food from abroad had to cross seas full of enemy submarines, and the country could not feed itself. Families were asked to turn their lawns into vegetable beds, and parks, playing fields and even the dry moat of the Tower of London were dug up and planted. Posters spoke of gardeners as soldiers on a home front; if the country was an army, every family with a spade was a platoon. In the United States, people planted what they called victory gardens, and by 1943 there were millions of them. Eleanor Roosevelt, a crusader for many causes, planted one at the White House, and the government hoped that every household would become a crusader for its own food.

Gardening was presented as part of the struggle against fascism. A row of beans could not defeat fascism by itself, of course, but it saved space on ships and freed money and farmland for the war, and food rationing in Britain lasted until 1954.

The work was not glamorous. Lettuce is easy to grow but hard to protect, and wartime gardeners fought slugs as fiercely as any modern gardener. A single slug can eat a young lettuce overnight. Gardeners also learned to watch for blight, a disease that can infect potato and tomato plants in wet weather and spread quickly from one garden to the next. If it infects one plant, the plant must be removed at once.

One wartime story about vegetables is still repeated. The government in London praised carrots as good for seeing in the dark, and newspapers suggested that a famous night pilot owed his success to them. According to the story, this was partly a hoax to hide the real secret: radar, which uses electromagnetic waves to find aircraft in the dark. Historians debate how deliberate the hoax was, but the electromagnetic secret was real, and carrots, though healthy, will not give anyone the eyes of a cat.

This spring our club planted lettuce along the fence, and we put out traps for every slug we could find. Our questionnaire did not ask about history, but next year I think it will.

Questions:
What does the community garden send its members every spring?
It sends a questionnaire about what they plan to grow and why they garden.
Why did Britain begin the Dig for Victory campaign?
Food from abroad had to cross seas full of submarines, and the country could not feed itself.
How did the posters describe gardeners?
They spoke of gardeners as soldiers, and of every family with a spade as a platoon.
What did Eleanor Roosevelt do?
